text: The envelope from the clinic is on the counter where I set it an hour ago and I have walked past it four times. It is thin, which could mean anything. My hands are cold and I keep them in my sleeves and do not pick it up.

The meeting invite arrived at four fifty on Friday with no agenda and two people from human resources on it, and it is Sunday night. I have reread the subject line until it means nothing. My stomach has been a fist since I saw it.

The vet's number is on the screen and the phone is ringing and I know what she is going to say about the bloodwork because of how she said tomorrow. I let it ring twice more. My thumb is over the green button and will not come down.

The exam hall doors are closed and we are lined up in the corridor and someone ahead of me is laughing too loud. My mouth is dry and the pencil case is slick in my hand. The doors will open in four minutes and I can feel each one of them.

The captain comes on and says we are going to hit some rough air and asks the crew to be seated, and the crew's faces do a thing. I tighten the belt that is already tight. The woman beside me puts her book down and we both look at the wing.

The hearing is at nine tomorrow and the suit is on the back of the door and I am lying on my back watching the ceiling fan go around. Every time I close my eyes the courtroom is there. The alarm is set and I will not need it.

The review is in thirty minutes and my manager has been in her office with the door shut since lunch, which she never does. I have opened and closed the same document six times. My coffee has gone cold and my hands have gone with it.
The drill whines from behind the door of the exam room and the chair I am waiting in faces that door. The receptionist smiles at me and I try to smile back. My tongue keeps finding the tooth.

The phone rings at three in the morning and the screen says my brother's name, and my brother does not call at three in the morning. I sit up and the room is very cold. I answer on the fourth ring because the first three were not possible.

The rumor has been going around since Monday and today the directors have been in the glass room all morning with the blinds down. People are typing without looking at their screens. I have a knot under my ribs that tightens each time the door opens.

The conference is at four and the teacher's email said she wanted to discuss some concerns, and the word concerns has been sitting in my chest all day. I park and do not get out. The hallway inside smells like it did when I was eight.

The results portal updates at noon and it is eleven fifty-two and the page is open on my phone and I have not refreshed it. The kitchen is very quiet. I pick up the phone and put it down and pick it up.

The examiner gets into the passenger seat with the clipboard and says pull out when you are ready, and I am not ready and the car is already in reverse. My foot is shaking on the brake. The parking lot has never looked so full of things to hit.

The attic hatch is open above me and the flashlight beam goes up into the dark and the noise has stopped, which is worse than when it was going. The ladder is cold under my hands. I put one foot on the first rung and wait there.

The letter from the tax office has the kind of window envelope that is never good news and it is addressed to me by my full legal name. I turn it over and over. The kitchen clock is loud and the letter stays sealed.

The nurse said the doctor would call back this afternoon and it is four thirty and the phone is on the table face up. Each time it buzzes with something else my whole body jumps and then settles into something heavier. I have not left the room.

The police tape is gone from the door and the locksmith has been and it is time to go back into the house. My key is in the lock and I have not turned it. Whatever they touched is still in there in the order they left it.

Tomorrow is the first day back after three months and the badge is on the counter and the laptop is charged and I have laid out clothes like a child. Everyone will ask how I am. I lie in the dark and rehearse a sentence I do not believe.

The knock comes at eleven at night, three slow knocks, and no one who knows us knocks like that. My husband and I look at each other across the living room. I am standing before I know I have stood and my legs are not sure about it.

The tech has gone quiet and is moving the wand back and forth over the same spot and the screen is turned away from me. The gel is cold on my stomach. I am watching her face because it is the only thing I can read.

The text says we need to talk and nothing else and she is not answering the follow-up. I am in the car outside the office with the engine running. The drive home is twenty minutes and I am not sure I want it to be shorter.

The dog's limp was better yesterday and worse this morning and the appointment is at two and he is lying by the door with his head on his paws. I sit on the floor next to him and do not look at the clock. My hand on his side is counting his breaths.

The warning light came on forty miles ago and the next town is sixty more and the engine has started making a sound underneath the radio. I turn the radio off. Every mile marker is a small victory I do not trust.

The tracks in the mud are fresh and wide and the claw marks are as long as my fingers and the trail goes exactly where they go. I stand still with my pack straps in both fists. The woods ahead have gone very quiet.

The ice ahead is a different color, grayer, with a line of open water beyond it, and the shore is behind me and the shortcut is in front. I slide one boot forward and the ice talks back. My breath has gone shallow and high in my chest.

The parking garage is empty at this hour and my car is on the fourth level and the elevator is out of order again. My footsteps come back to me off the concrete. I hold my keys between my fingers and do not run because running would mean something.

Surgery is at seven and it is five and I am sitting on the edge of the hospital bed in the gown with the strings that do not tie. The hallway outside is beginning to wake up. My hands are folded so they will stop doing other things.

I am third on the program and the second speaker is wrapping up and my slides are loaded and my throat has closed to a straw. The audience is four hundred dim shapes. I stand up before my name is called because sitting is worse.

The cruiser has been behind me for six blocks, matching my turns, and the registration expired last week and I know it. I keep both hands on the wheel and my eyes on the mirror more than the road. Any second now the lights will come on.
The bank's number is on the screen and the overdraft letter is beside the phone and I have to make this call before five. My thumb hovers. The hold music will be the easy part.

The school nurse left a message saying nothing was wrong but could I call, and nothing was wrong is a phrase that means something is. I am dialing from the car in the grocery lot. Each ring is longer than the one before.

The walk from my office to hers is forty steps and I am going to tell her the position is being eliminated and I have practiced the sentence and it is still the wrong sentence. Her door is open. I slow down for the last ten steps and it does not help.
The best man is standing and tapping his glass and I am next and the cards in my pocket are damp from my hand. Two hundred faces will turn. I take a sip of water that goes down the wrong way.

The forecast has the river cresting Thursday at a number two feet above the top of our sandbags and it is Tuesday night. I am standing at the back window watching water I cannot see yet. The pump is running and I keep listening for it to stop.

The basement lights are out and the breaker box is at the far end past the furnace and the flashlight is dimmer than it was last time. I go down three steps and stop. The dark down there has a shape and I am waiting for it to move.

The last contraction ended two minutes ago and the next one is coming, I can feel it building the way the last one did, and the last one was the worst so far. I grip the bed rail. The nurse says you are doing great and I do not believe her.
The proctor is walking down the rows with the booklets face down and she is two desks away. My pencils are lined up. My heart is going slow and hard like something knocking to be let out.

The coach is pinning the roster to the board and the whole team is pretending not to crowd toward it. I am at the back with my bag on my shoulder. The list is one sheet and my name is either on it or it is not and I cannot make my feet move.

The vet has taken the cat into the back and said she would be a few minutes and it has been twenty, and when it is nothing it is never twenty. The exam room has a poster about fleas. I read it for the fourth time.

The waiting room on the third floor has softer chairs than the others, and I know why, and I am sitting in one. My name will be called and a door will open and a man in a white coat will sit down slowly. I hold my coat in my lap like something that might get away.

The ladder flexes with every rung and the gutter is still four feet above me and the ground is a long way down and getting longer. I stop climbing. My hands are locked around the rails and I can feel my pulse in them.

The noise under the hood started as a tick and is now a knock and it is dark and the road has no shoulder. I turn the radio off to hear it better and wish I had not. The next exit sign says nineteen miles.

The school bus is three stops away and he is standing at the curb with the backpack that is bigger than his torso and I am holding his hand harder than he is holding mine. He has never been anywhere without me for six hours. My throat has something in it that will not go down.

The recital program has my daughter fourth and the third kid is halfway through and I am in the second row with my hands pressed between my knees. She looked at me once from the wings. I cannot play the piano for her and I want to.

The email went to the whole company instead of to Dan and I saw it a second after I hit send and the replies have not started yet. I am watching the inbox. Each new message that is not about it is a small reprieve I do not trust.

The test is on the bathroom counter and the timer on my phone says ninety seconds and I am sitting on the edge of the tub not looking at it. Either answer changes everything. My hands are between my knees and the fan is loud.

The lab portal is loading, the little wheel turning, and the result will be a number and I know which side of the line the number has to fall on. The wheel keeps turning. I have stopped breathing in a way I do not notice until my chest hurts.

The machine is a tube and the tech says it will take forty minutes and to hold still, and the table slides in with me on it. The ceiling is six inches from my face. The first bang comes and my whole body wants to be somewhere else.

The check-engine light is flashing, not steady, flashing, and the manual says that means pull over now and the shoulder is gravel on a curve. I am slowing down with the hazards on. The trucks behind me are not slowing down.

The principal's office is at the end of the hall and the secretary said he will see you now and I am an adult and my palms are sweating anyway. The hall is lined with children's drawings. I knock on the open door because my hand needs something to do.

The elevator is going down to the garage where my car is parked next to his, and his shift ends at the same time mine does, and the doors are closing. I press the button for the lobby instead and it does not light. The numbers go down one at a time.

The adoption agency said they would call by the end of the week with the committee's decision and it is Friday at four. My wife is at the window and I am at the table and neither of us is talking. The phone sits between us like a third person.

The smoke on the horizon has gone from a smudge to a wall since lunch and the evacuation map puts our road in the yellow band that touches the orange. The go bags are by the door. I keep walking to the window and the wall is closer each time.

The judge has gone back to chambers and the lawyers are whispering and I am on the bench with my hands clamped between my knees. The clock above the door has no second hand. When the side door opens I will know from her face.

The biopsy was Monday and they said a week and it is Friday and every time the phone rings I know, and then it is my mother, and then it is a survey. I have stopped answering with hello. The weekend is a hallway with no doors.

The climbing rope is rigged and the edge of the cliff is three feet away and below it is nothing for a hundred feet, and it is my turn to lean back into the harness. My knees have gone to water. The instructor says I have you and the words do not reach my hands.
